inline.s: Recorded by Fushan, attendant of the Narayana Cave of the Eastern Sea
Annotated by Fuzheng, a disciple of the Kaiyuan Prefectural Office in Wu-Yue
The twenty-fifth year of the Jiajing reign of the Ming emperor Shizong (Su), the cyclical year Bingwu

I was a man of Quanjiao County in Jinling, of the Cai clan. My father was named Yan Gao, and my mother was of the Hong clan, who in her whole life venerated the Great Being Avalokitesvara. At first she dreamed that the Great Being led a boy into the house; my mother received and embraced him, and so became pregnant. At birth he came forth wrapped in white garments and a double membrane. He was born in the tenth month of that year, on the twelfth day, in the Jichou hour. (Seen once by the father, once by the mother.)

The disciple Guanheng of Zhuanyu, in his Biography of the Reviving Master Han of Caoxi, says: The Master's name was Deqing, his style Cheng-yin, his other title Hanshan. When his mother loosed him from her womb he came forth wrapped in white garments; when the clothes were removed for his bathing, the water gave off a strange fragrance. After he left home at the Bao'en Temple, one day before the relic stupa he met an Indian monk, who said: 'This young master will in a future day turn the great Wheel of Dharma; his mouth is like a full moon rising â€” it is the mouth of a Buddha.' Again, in the temple corridor he met a man who said: 'Yao's brows had eight colors; your brows have five colors, and you bear the charge of the three teachings.' Later at Mount Wutai, passing through the Great Stupa Temple while he was an ascetic, he met a monk of imposing appearance who took him by the hand and said: 'Master, you are a great man reborn; your whole head of hair is a dark purplish blue, and you will surely do great work for the Buddha.'
O
Fuzheng's note:

The chronicle records: in the forty-second year of the Wanli reign, the cyclical year Jiayin, in the eleventh month, the disciple Wuxin Zhuanyu came to pay his respects. In the Collected Works of Hanshan's Journey of Dreams there is a Dharma-discourse given to the Chan practitioner Zhuanyu Heng. It says in brief: Zhuanyu first followed the Great Master Kongyin of Mount Wutai, listening to and studying the sutras and treatises. After a long time he set them all aside, raised a single thought, and earnestly investigated his own fundamental affair. Traveling ten thousand li south, he passed Caoxi and called upon the Elder to seek correction. The Elder showed him the path of turning about; he assented, bowed, and took his leave, then went to dwell on Mount Heng. Before long the Elder also arrived. The practitioner went to Baoqing for medical help because of illness, and the Elder lamented that true students who take birth-and-death as their concern are the rarest in the Chan school. On the first day of the third month of the year Bingchen, in the wind and rain at midnight, the practitioner all at once came through the rain and mud. Seeing that his illness had healed, the Elder was overjoyed. He again offered incense and sought correction, and the Elder admonished him: 'Your bodily sickness has healed; you must never let the sickness of Chan afflict you. The ancients said: to let go of emotion is easy, to let go of Dharma is hard. The practitioner's letting go of body is letting go of emotion; his letting go of views is letting go of Dharma. When both emotion and Dharma are forgotten, is he not a great unhindered, liberated person?' This discourse runs to several thousand characters. In the collected works few are praised so highly, so the writing of a biography of the revival is warranted. What I find fault with is that the biography is full of errors, which may easily mislead later students. Since he called but twice for correction, and only at one time, his days of following were few; he later never saw the self-authored chronicle, so what he heard was told variously and the discrepancy is not small. Now I take the chronicle as the main text and supplement it with one or two urgent anecdotes and sayings from the biography, such as the whole account of the hermit of Mount Panshan, which is most beneficial. Other baseless digressions I have all deleted. By and large the defect of Chan lies in running toward the school and shunning the doctrine; [the author] does not realize that Patriarch Han and the Sixth Patriarch were both upholders of school and doctrine together, both manifested flesh-bodies at Caoxi, and both had no single transmission of robe and bowl. The Dharma-descendant grandson Suhua Zhixu, whose first affinity and resolve arose from being received in a dream, united school and doctrine in one body in his own age. He made the Record in Praise of the Eighteen Patriarchs, ending with Patriarch Han. The Eighteen Patriarchs are those who did not transmit the robe and bowl; and the one biography of Patriarch Han condenses the biography of Zhuanyu, exactly matching the chronicle; he should be counted a worthy of the private tradition.
O
A flesh-body Buddha and patriarch â€” the model of his coming into the world was already in the mother's womb. The supreme causes of his many kalpas were no small matter.
The twenty-sixth year, the cyclical year Dingwei

When I was one full year old, a wind-ailment struck me and I nearly died. My mother prayed to the Great Being and so vowed to give me up to become a monk; I was registered under the Changshou Temple of the town, and my milk-name was changed to 'Monk.' (Seen a second time by the mother.)

Fuzheng recites that the milk-name 'Damei' was later perfectly fulfilled. One must know that the Dharma-name Deqing came from Grandmaster Xilin, given at the time of leaving home; the chronicle does not record it. The name given by his father, before it was changed, is likewise not recorded.
The twenty-seventh year, the cyclical year Wushen
When I was three, I often sat alone and did not like to play with the other children. My grandfather often said: 'This child is like a wooden post.' (Seen once by the grandfather.)
Fuzheng observes: having at last attained that very post [of the image], the grandfather may be said to have had an eye of discernment.
The twenty-eighth year, the cyclical year Jiyou; the twenty-ninth year, Gengxu; the thirtieth year, Xinhai; the thirty-first year, Renzi

When I was seven, my uncle was very fond of me. My mother first sent me to the village school. One day my uncle died and lay on the bed. When I came home my mother deceived me, saying: 'Your uncle is sleeping; you may call him to wake.' I called him several times, and my aunt, struck with grief, wept: 'Oh heaven, where has he gone?' Startled, I doubted, and asked my mother: 'Uncle's body is here â€” where then has he gone?' My mother said: 'Your uncle is dead.' I asked: 'When one dies, where does one go?' Thence I doubted deeply. Before long, my second aunt gave birth to a boy and my mother went to see, with me following. Seeing the baby, so small, I asked my mother: 'How did this child enter my aunt's belly?' My mother slapped me and said: 'Foolish child â€” how did you enter your mother's belly?' Again I doubted deeply. From this the doubt of dying and being born could not be resolved from my breast. (Seen a third time by the mother, and once each by the uncle, the aunt, and the younger brother.)

Fuzheng's note: This seven-year-old child â€” how did he come by this bone-and-marrow crisis of death and life? Mother and son, face to face, cross-examining such a great mass of doubt â€” an extremely wonderful case. Appearing in person like the mother of the Buddha, a brand-new hammer and tongs to cook down Buddhas and refine patriarchs â€” the foremost great case.
The thirty-second year, the cyclical year Guichou

When I was eight, I studied and boarded with in-laws across the river. My mother warned me not to come back; I was to return only once a month. One day I came home and, clinging to her, would not leave; my mother was angry, whipped me, and drove me to the riverbank, yet I would not board the boat. In anger she seized my topknot and flung me into the river, then turned and went home without a glance. My grandmother saw it, called out for me to be pulled out, and sent me home. My mother said: 'This worthless child â€” if he was not drowned, why keep him?' She beat me and drove me off again, showing not the least attachment. At the time I thought to myself that my mother's heart was cruel, and from then on I did not long for home. My mother was often in tears across the river, and my grandmother scolded her. My mother said: 'It is right to cut off love for him â€” only then can he study.' (Seen once by the grandmother, a fourth time by the mother.)

Reading to this point, Fuzheng's tears flood at every word and sentence. One who could read it without tears is not human. With palms together he praises: 'How compassionate, how merciful, how good, how faithful! Such being so, how could the mother not cast away her child? How could he not carve his flesh to repay his mother?'
The thirty-third year, the cyclical year Jiayin

When I was nine, studying at the temple, I heard a monk reciting the Avalokitesvara Sutra, which can save the world from suffering. Overjoyed, I asked the monk for the text, read it in secret, and could at once recite it. My mother venerated the Great Being Avalokitesvara, and whenever she burned incense and bowed I always followed. One day I said to my mother: 'The Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara has a scroll of scripture.' She said: 'I do not know of it.' I recited it once for my mother, and she said, delighted: 'Where did you get this? The sound of your recitation is like that of an old master.' (Seen a fifth time by the mother.)

Qian Muzhai Qianyi composed the Stupa Inscription for Great Master Hanshan at Wuru Peak, Mount Lu. He says that when the Master was nine he could recite the Universal Gate Chapter, which is what the chronicle calls the Avalokitesvara Sutra. In the cyclical year Dingmao of the Tianqi reign, Chen Dixiang of Nanhai and Fushan, a disciple of Wuru, entrusted the account of conduct to Muzhai for the stupa inscription; and the affair of reviving Caoxi he seems to have heard partly from Xiao Xuanpu of Xuanhua. But the details of the journey east, not fully known from first to last, differ greatly from the chronicle. Now the flesh-body is at Caoxi, and the Wuru Peak stupa inscription is indeed lost; of its sources scarcely a tenth can be recovered.
O

Fuzheng, reading this, understands that to win an examination degree and become an official, one need not truly study; but for right understanding and views â€” to become a Buddha or a patriarch â€” there is no one who does not begin with true study. This very scroll of the Avalokitesvara Sutra, memorized in early youth, came wholly through study as its condition; and by reciting it once for his mother he could repay his mother's kindness in driving him away.
The thirty-fourth year, the cyclical year Yimao

When I was ten, my mother pressed my studies very strictly and I found it laborious. So I asked my mother: 'What is the use of studying?' She said: 'To become an official.' I asked: 'What kind of official?' She said: 'Begin with a small post; if you are capable, you may reach the prime ministership.' I asked: 'Having become prime minister, what then?' She said: 'That is all.' I said: 'What a pity â€” a whole life of toil and at last that is all! What is the use of it? I think one should only do something that is not 'all there is'.' She said: 'A worthless child like you can only be a wandering monk.' I said: 'What is a wandering monk, and what good is in it?' She said: 'A monk is a disciple of the Buddha, traveling the whole world, free and at ease, provided for wherever he goes.' I said: 'That is just right for me.' She said: 'I only fear you lack the good fortune for it.' I said: 'Why must there be good fortune?' She said: 'In the world those who become the top scholar are common; but to leave home and become a Buddha or a patriarch â€” is that not rare?' I said: 'If I have the good fortune, I fear only that my mother cannot let me go.' She said: 'If you have the good fortune, then I can let you go.' I kept this in mind. (Seen a sixth time by the mother.)

Fuzheng sighs; oh, oh! Mother and son, sitting close together, speaking of the birthless. The instruction was so clear, the pointing so broad, the keen edge so sharp, the taking-up so quick. At ten, the mother in Jinling gave up her son's flesh-body; at seventy-eight, the son's flesh-body at Caoxi repaid his mother. A veritable great cause-and-condition, truly most wondrous!
The thirty-fifth year, the cyclical year Bingchen
